source.title: Scaling laws for single-agent reinforcement learning
source.authors: Jacob Hilton; Jie Tang; John D. Schulman

record.file_problem: None noted; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling relationships in a new training regime, single-agent reinforcement learning, using intrinsic performance rather than held-out cross-entropy loss.
record.gate_note: The paper does not measure language-model cross-entropy, language-model scaling, or downstream language-task performance. Its direct results are fitted power laws for RL intrinsic performance and derived optimal model size versus compute. It also reports a horizon-length/sample-efficiency result listed under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study fits the Kaplan-form power law (eq. 1) in model size and environment interactions for single-agent RL, a new training regime (V5). It derives optimal model size versus compute and reports how exponents and coefficients vary with environment, horizon, training period, width versus depth, parameter counting and metric choice (V7). The measure is intrinsic performance, not cross-entropy. Intrinsic performance makes the compute-frontier power law true by definition, so only the N/E functional form and its exponents are substantive.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that intrinsic performance follows an approximate power law in model size and environment interactions across environments, so optimal model size scales as a power law in compute (exponent roughly 0.4–0.8). Coefficients vary by orders of magnitude, and horizon length mostly changes the coefficient, not the exponent. They stress that precise exponents are uncertain, given no per-budget learning-rate schedules, under-training and noise. They call their results inconclusive on whether the exponent is about 0.5 in every domain.
record.recipe_differences: Uses single-agent RL training and an intrinsic-performance metric defined from compute-efficient frontiers, rather than language-model pretraining and held-out cross-entropy loss.
record.method_sensitivity: Fitted exponents vary by domain and environment, training period, task horizon, and width versus depth scaling. Alternative Dota 2 performance-metric fits also yield different derived exponents. The authors identify learning-rate schedules, under-training, model aspect ratios, and fitting/data limitations as possible influences.

fits_no_version.finding: MNIST interactions needed for 99% training accuracy grow approximately affinely with horizon length, with deviations at short horizons and for large models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In independent-timestep RL, sample requirements for a fixed performance level are an affine function of the credit-assignment horizon.

record.problems: The authors report uncertainty in fitted exponents; no separate training run and learning-rate schedule was used for each compute budget; some models were under-trained relative to the compute-efficient frontier; model aspect ratios were not carefully optimized; RL learning curves remained noisy; Dota 2 used one seed; and depth-scaling parameter/FLOP calculations omit the final dense layer and introduce further approximation.

untested.parts: No language-model held-out cross-entropy; the study is RL only.
Section 5.1 extrapolates the infinite-width limit, but no prediction of larger runs is checked against actual larger runs.
No language-model loss-minimising N/D split. The RL analog is captured under V5 and V7.
Width and depth are scaled separately; there is no fixed-parameter-count comparison of shapes.
Image, video, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer are not tested. Only RL with an intrinsic-performance metric is covered.

missing.what: Parameter-counting dependence. Depth-scaling optimal model size is much smaller than width scaling because the final dense layer is excluded (16–90% of parameters). The curves become similar when size is measured in FLOPs per forward pass.
CoinRun fail-to-success-ratio fits give optimal-size exponents 0.5285 (easy) and 0.4822 (hard), versus intrinsic-performance 0.4600 and 0.4315.

Optimal-size coefficient varies by orders of magnitude across domains: Dota needs about 2,000× longer training than MNIST horizon 1 at similar exponents. RL optimal sizes are smaller than generative modeling.
Seed-level variation of Procgen αN and αE (per-seed fitted values plotted).

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The study tests the claim's RL analog using a metric defined via the compute-efficient frontier, so 'power law in compute' holds by construction. The evidence lies in the N/E form and the derived exponents. Rows R14–R16 are linked to V7 only, since they compare fitting choices. Learning-rate schedules were not re-tuned per budget, which echoes the Hoffmann critique of Kaplan; this may bias the exponents.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss or language-model parameter, token, or compute sweep.
No test of whether power laws fitted on small language-model runs predict much larger runs.
The paper derives optimal model size versus compute for RL using environment interactions and intrinsic performance, not loss-minimising language-model parameter and token counts.
Width and depth scaling are explored, but the study does not compare architectures at a fixed parameter count to measure how much architecture details change loss.
Tests RL intrinsic performance, not cross-entropy loss; does not test image/video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
No downstream-task performance prediction from pretraining loss or scale.
Examines dependence on RL environment, horizon, training period, and scaling width versus depth. Does not test language-model parameter-counting choices or the specific Kaplan–Hoffmann disagreement.

relationships.condition: Procgen (width and depth), Dota 2 1v1, MNIST RL, late period
relationships.reason: Eq. 1 (Kaplan form, with I^-β in place of loss) fits learning curves across all environments, giving power-law optimal size versus compute (R1–R13, R17–R26).
relationships.display_finding: A Kaplan-form relationship using I^−β in place of loss fit learning curves across all environments and implied power-law optimal model size versus compute.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Procgen (width and depth), Dota 2 1v1, MNIST RL, late period
source_check.reason: Equation 1 approximately fits intrinsic performance across these RL settings; the optimal-size power laws follow from those fits.

relationships.condition: Early training; constructed metric; depth scaling
relationships.reason: A good fit requires excluding an early transient, with αE lower early and mid-training (R27, R28). The metric is intrinsic performance, built so the compute frontier is a power law by construction. Depth fits are noisier (R7–R12).
relationships.display_finding: Good fits required excluding an early transient, with lower αE early and midway through training; the intrinsic-performance metric imposed a power-law compute frontier by construction, and depth fits were noisier.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Early training; constructed metric; depth scaling
source_check.reason: Section 4.3 explicitly requires excluding an initial transient for good fits. The compute frontier is fixed by the intrinsic-performance definition; depth fits retain the law with greater noise.

relationships.condition: Across domains, environments, width versus depth, MNIST training period
relationships.reason: The optimal-size exponent ranges 0.40–0.65 (Procgen), 0.66–0.80 (MNIST) and 0.76 (Dota). Depth and width exponents show no clear relation. αE shifts with training period (R1–R13, R27, R28).
relationships.display_finding: Optimal-size exponents range from 0.40 to 0.65 for Procgen and 0.66 to 0.80 for MNIST, with 0.76 for Dota, while width and depth exponents show no clear relationship and αE changes with training period.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Across domains, environments, width versus depth, MNIST training period
source_check.reason: Fitted exponents vary across environments, architecture scaling and training periods. Parameter counting also affects allocation coefficients, although precise exponents remain uncertain.

relationships.reason: Horizon mainly shifts the optimal-size coefficient (the curve moves right). The exponent drop 0.80→0.66 is attributed to under-training rather than a true change (R17–R26).
relationships.display_finding: Longer horizons mainly shift the optimal-size coefficient, while the exponent decrease from 0.80 to 0.66 is attributed to under-training.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.reason: Horizon changes the compute-optimal allocation mainly through its coefficient. Sections 4.2–4.3 identify under-training as a confound for the apparent exponent decrease.
